mantellisaurus:enwiki:3.title: Mantellisaurus (Discovery and naming of the holotype)

facts.statement: Mantellisaurus lived during the Early Cretaceous, specifically from the Barremian to the early Aptian ages.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Early Cretaceous, Barremian to early Aptian

facts.statement: This iguanodontian dinosaur lived in Europe during the Barremian and early Aptian stages of the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Mantellisaurus is a genus of iguanodontian dinosaur that lived in the Barremian and early Aptian ages of the Early Cretaceous Period of Europe.

facts.statement: Fossil remains of Mantellisaurus have been found in Belgium, England, Spain, and Germany.
facts.quote: Its remains are known from Belgium (Bernissart), England, Spain and Germany.

facts.statement: The genus contains only one species, Mantellisaurus atherfieldensis.
facts.quote: The type and only species is M. atherfieldensis.

facts.statement: Gregory Paul established the genus Mantellisaurus in 2007, separating it from Iguanodon atherfieldensis.
facts.quote: Formerly known as Iguanodon atherfieldensis, the new genus Mantellisaurus was erected for the species by Gregory Paul in 2007.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen was discovered by Reginald Walter Hooley in 1914 in southern England and reported in 1917.
facts.quote: The holotype fossil, NHMUK PV R5764, was originally discovered by Reginald Walter Hooley in 1914 in the upper Vectis Formation of southern England and reported upon in 1917.

facts.statement: Reginald Walter Hooley named the species Iguanodon atherfieldensis in 1925, after his death.
facts.quote: He posthumously named it Iguanodon atherfieldensis in 1925.

facts.statement: The species name 'atherfieldensis' refers to the village of Atherfield on the Isle of Wight where the fossil was found.
facts.quote: Atherfield is the name of a village on the southwest shore of the Isle of Wight where the fossil was found.

facts.statement: A significant specimen was discovered in a quarry in Maidstone, Kent, in February 1834.
facts.quote: The Maidstone specimen was discovered in a quarry in Maidstone, Kent, owned by William Harding Bensted, in February 1834 (lower Lower Greensand Formation).

facts.statement: Gideon Mantell purchased the Maidstone specimen for £25 in June 1834.
facts.quote: In June 1834 it was acquired for £25 by scientist Gideon Mantell.

facts.statement: Gideon Mantell identified the Maidstone specimen as an Iguanodon based on its distinctive teeth.
facts.quote: He was led to identify it as an Iguanodon based on its distinctive teeth.

facts.statement: Mantell incorrectly placed a horn on the nose of the Iguanodon reconstruction based on this specimen.
facts.quote: the most famous of which was the placement of what he thought was a horn on the nose.

facts.statement: Tension arose between Gideon Mantell and Richard Owen shortly after the discovery of the Maidstone specimen.
facts.quote: Shortly after the discovery, tension began to build between Mantell and Richard Owen, an ambitious scientist with much better funding and society connections in the turbulent worlds of Reform Act–era British politics and science.

facts.statement: Before his death in 1852, Mantell realized that Mantellodon had slender forelimbs rather than being a heavy, pachyderm-like animal.
facts.quote: In 1849, a few years before his death in 1852, Mantell realised that the genus today known as Mantellodon was not a heavy, pachyderm-like animal, as Owen was putting forward, but had slender forelimbs

facts.statement: Richard Owen included two Mantellodon sculptures, one standing and one resting, in his series of lifesize concrete dinosaur models.
facts.quote: With Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins, Owen had nearly two dozen lifesize sculptures of various prehistoric animals built out of concrete sculpted over a steel and brick framework; two Mantellodon, one standing and one resting on its belly, were included.

facts.statement: A banquet for twenty people was held inside the standing Mantellodon sculpture before it was completed.
facts.quote: Before the sculpture of the standing Mantellodon was completed, a banquet for twenty was held inside it.

facts.statement: Later discoveries revealed that the structure Mantell thought was a horn was actually a modified thumb.
facts.quote: The discovery of much better specimens of Iguanodon bernissartensis in later years revealed that the horn was actually a modified thumb.

facts.statement: The borough of Maidstone added an Iguanodon to its coat of arms in 1949 to commemorate the discovery.
facts.quote: The borough of Maidstone commemorated this find by adding an Iguanodon as a supporter to their coat of arms in 1949.

facts.statement: A sculpture nicknamed 'Iggy the Iguanodon' based on the Maidstone specimen was unveiled at Maidstone East station in 2021.
facts.quote: In 2021, a sculpture nicknamed Iggy the Iguanodon based on the Maidstone specimen was unveiled at the Maidstone East station.

facts.statement: The Iguanodon is the only dinosaur featured in a UK borough's coat of arms.
facts.quote: The dinosaur is also featured in Maidstone's coat of arms, and is the only dinosaur featured in a borough's coat of arms in the UK.

facts.statement: Specimen IRSNB 1551 became the second mounted non-avian dinosaur skeleton made primarily of actual bone when displayed by Louis Dollo in 1884.
facts.quote: Specimen IRSNB 1551 from the Sainte-Barbe Clays, Belgium, became the second mounted skeleton of a non-avian dinosaur made primarily out of actual bone when put on display by Louis Dollo in 1884.

facts.statement: This Belgian specimen was originally assigned to Iguanodon mantelli in 1881 but was later thought to belong to Iguanodon atherfieldensis in 1986.
facts.quote: This specimen was originally assigned to Iguanodon mantelli by George Albert Boulenger in 1881, but was in 1986 thought to pertain to Iguanodon atherfieldensis by David Bruce Norman.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul assigned this specimen to the genus and species Dollodon bampingi in 2008.
facts.quote: The specimen was assigned to its own genus and species, Dollodon bampingi, by Gregory S. Paul in 2008.

facts.statement: In 2010, Kenneth Carpenter and Yusuke Ishida synonymized Dollodon bampingi with Iguanodon seelyi.
facts.quote: In 2010, Kenneth Carpenter and Yusuke Ishida synonymized Dollodon bampingi with Iguanodon seelyi, a species based on BMNH R 28685 from Wessex Formation, England.

facts.statement: In 1971, a quarry near Nehden, Germany, yielded numerous disarticulated iguanodontid remains, mostly Mantellisaurus, alongside other dinosaur and crocodylian fragments.
facts.quote: In 1971, a fossiliferous karstic sinkhole clay deposit was found at a quarry just south-west of the village of Nehden near Brilon in Sauerland, Germany containing numerous disarticulated iguanodontid remains predominantly of Mantellisaurus with lesser quantities of Iguanodon, alongside other fragmentary dinosaur and crocodylian material.

facts.statement: Mantellisaurus fossils are known from several localities in Spain, including an articulated hindlimb from Las Hoyas and a specimen from Rubielos de Mora.
facts.quote: Mantellisaurus is known from several localities in Spain, with an articulated hindlimb known from Las Hoyas and a specimen known from the Rubielos de Mora 1 locality in Spain.

facts.statement: Three Mantellisaurus specimens are known from the Arcillas de Morella Formation in Spain.
facts.quote: Three specimens are known from the Arcillas de Morella Formation.

facts.statement: The genus name Mantellisaurus honors Gideon Mantell, the discoverer of Iguanodon.
facts.quote: The genus name honours Gideon Mantell, the discoverer of Iguanodon.

facts.statement: Mantellisaurus was a lightly constructed iguanodontian dinosaur.
facts.quote: Mantellisaurus was a lightly constructed iguanodont.

facts.statement: Mantellisaurus was smaller than Iguanodon bernissartensis, with an estimated weight of 750 kg.
facts.quote: Compared to Iguanodon bernissartensis, Mantellisaurus was smaller, estimated at 750 kg in weight.

facts.statement: The forelimbs of Mantellisaurus were proportionally shorter than those of Iguanodon bernissartensis.
facts.quote: Its forelimbs were proportionally shorter than those of I. bernissartensis.

facts.statement: Gregory Paul proposed that Mantellisaurus was primarily bipedal, using all fours only when standing still or moving slowly.
facts.quote: Due to the short length of its forelimbs and the shortness of its body, Paul proposed that it was primarily bipedal, only going on all fours when standing still or moving slowly.

facts.statement: The validity of the genus Dollodon is disputed among researchers.
facts.quote: The validity of Dollodon has since been disputed.

facts.statement: The holotype fossils of Mantellisaurus were discovered in 1917 by Reginald Hooley in Atherfield on the Isle of Wight, England.
facts.quote: Los fósiles del holotipo, NHMUK R5764, fueron descubiertos en 1917 por Reginald Hooley en Atherfield, al sudoeste de la isla de Wight, Inglaterra.

facts.statement: Reginald Hooley named the species Iguanodon atherfieldensis in 1925, after his death.
facts.quote: Lo llamó póstumamente Iguanodon atherfieldensis en 1925.

facts.statement: Mantellisaurus reached a length of 7 meters and a weight of 750 kilograms.
facts.quote: Alcanzó los 7 metros de largo y 750 kilogramos de peso.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul proposed that Mantellisaurus was primarily bipedal, using four legs only when standing or moving slowly.
facts.quote: Paul propuso que era principalmente bípedo, solo a cuatro patas cuando estaba parado o moviéndose lentamente.

facts.statement: Mantellisaurus lived during the mid-Cretaceous, approximately 125 million years ago, between the Barremian and Aptian stages in what is now Europe.
facts.quote: que vivió a mediados del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 125 millones de años, entre el Barremiense y el Aptiense, en lo que hoy es Europa.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul recognized Mantellisaurus as a distinct dinosaur genus in 2006.
facts.quote: No fue hasta 2006 que Gregory S. Paul lo reconoció como un nuevo tipo de dinosaurio.

facts.statement: In 2012, Andrew McDonald considered Mantellisaurus atherfieldensis to be a synonym of Dollodon bampingi and possibly Proplanicoxa galtoni.
facts.quote: McDonald en 2012 reconoció a M. atherfieldensis como un antiguo sinónimo de Dollodon bampingi y probablemente también Proplanicoxa galtoni.

facts.statement: The validity of the genus Dollodon has been disputed since its description.
facts.quote: La validez de Dollodon ha sido disputada desde entonces.

facts.statement: A 2010 cladistic analysis by McDonald, Barrett, and Chapman suggested that Mantellisaurus atherfieldensis is a sister taxon to Dollodon bampingi.
facts.quote: De un análisis cladista realizado por McDonald, Barrett y Chapman en 2010, se deduce que Mantellisaurus atherfieldensis es un taxón hermano de Dollodon bampingi

facts.statement: Both Mantellisaurus and Dollodon are considered the most basal representatives of the clade Hadrosauroidea, which includes hadrosaurids and taxa more closely related to them than to Iguanodon.
facts.quote: y que ambas especies son los representantes más basales del clado que incluye a los hadrosáuridos y todos los taxones que tienen un ancestro común más reciente con ellos que el de Iguanodon, es decir, el clado Hadrosauroidea según Sereno en 2005.

facts.statement: The time range for Mantellisaurus is recorded from the Berriasian to the Aptian, spanning from 143.1 to 119.57 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Berriasian to Aptian (143.1 to 119.57 million years ago)
